dropped.label: ci-cache-key-literal-backslash
dropped.reason: I first read `key: suite-\${{ env.APISGURU_COMMIT }}` as an escaped expression that would leave the cache key constant, so the fixture cache would never invalidate. GitHub Actions has no backslash escape for `${{`; the documented escape is `${{ '${{' }}`. The runner therefore still interpolates the expression and the key varies with APISGURU_COMMIT, carrying only a stray leading backslash. Cosmetic, not a cache-poisoning or staleness defect.

dropped.label: gorillamux-makeservers-nil-server-variable-panic
dropped.reason: makeServers dereferences `server.Variables[sVar].Default` and slices `rest[:rhs]` without checking that the variable is declared or that a closing brace exists, so a server URL such as `{host}` with no `variables` block would nil-dereference. Server.Validate rejects exactly that document before any router is built, and both the router's own doc comment and the README quickstart call doc.Validate first, so a validated document cannot reach the dereference.

dropped.label: isnilvalue-array-kind-reflect-panic
dropped.reason: isNilValue lists reflect.Array among the kinds it calls reflect.Value.IsNil() on, and IsNil panics for the Array kind. No producer on the path into it can emit a Go array: parsePrimitiveCase returns only int32, int64, float64, bool and string; parseArray and sliceMapToSlice return []any; makeObject returns map[string]any; the body decoders return string, []any, map[string]any or json.Number. The panic is unreachable from any attacker-controlled input, and the defect is latent rather than exploitable.

dropped.label: multipart-part-value-string-assertion
dropped.reason: MultipartBodyDecoder calls parsePrimitive(value.(string), ...) with an unchecked assertion when the part carries no Content-Type or text/plain. decodeBody rewrites an empty Content-Type to text/plain whenever the reader is a *multipart.Part, so that branch always resolves to PlainBodyDecoder, which returns a string; the only other reachable decoder for a binary schema is FileBodyDecoder, which also returns a string. An attacker cannot steer the value to a non-string type from the wire.

findings.title: Unchecked map type assertion in deepSet panics on deepObject query parameters that mix depths
findings.impact: An unauthenticated remote client aborts request validation with a Go panic on demand. Under a standard net/http server the panic is recovered per connection, so the effect is an aborted request, a closed connection and a stack trace written to the server log on every attempt - a cheap log-flooding and availability primitive. Where ValidateRequest runs outside the http handler goroutine - a worker goroutine, a gRPC gateway, a serverless handler, a CLI, or any framework that does not recover - the process terminates.
findings.preconditions: The served OpenAPI document declares at least one query parameter with `style: deepObject` and an object schema, and the request reaches openapi3filter.ValidateRequest (directly, through openapi3filter.Validator.Middleware, or through ValidationHandler). No authentication is needed if the operation has none; security requirements are validated before parameters, so an authenticated operation requires a valid credential first.
findings.recommendation: Make deepSet total rather than assuming shape: use the comma-ok form and return an error when an intermediate node is already a non-map value, e.g. `next, ok := m[key].(map[string]any); if !ok { return &ParseError{Kind: KindInvalidFormat, Reason: "conflicting object and scalar for the same property"} }`, and propagate that error out of makeObject so the request is rejected with 400 instead of panicking. Sorting props by key depth before calling deepSet would hide the crash but still silently drop one of the two conflicting values, so prefer the explicit error. Independently, consider a package-level policy that no attacker-reachable path in openapi3filter uses a single-value type assertion - the same class is latent at req_resp_decoder.go:1630 and openapi3/loader.go:744-1465.

triage.reason: No compensating control exists inside the module: `grep -rn 'recover()' --include='*.go' .` returns no hit in any of the 293 Go files. The net/http server's own per-connection recover sits outside the module and is skipped whenever validation runs in another goroutine, so it is a control a caller may forget, which FP-01 explicitly excludes.
The props keys are built from url.Values keys, i.e. the raw request query string, at req_resp_decoder.go:703-720.
A single-value type assertion in Go panics on mismatch; that is the language definition of the sink, not a framework behaviour that could differ by version.
req_resp_decoder.go is a non-test file in the published module path github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter; it is behind no build tag and no environment flag.
The boundary crossed is remote HTTP client to server process; the second principal is any client that can reach the validated endpoint.

The attacker gains a capability it did not hold: it terminates request processing at will, and terminates the process outright wherever validation is not run under net/http's recover. That is above informational, and it is capped at medium rather than high precisely because the most common deployment does recover.

findings.limits: Establishes a reachable panic, not memory corruption or any confidentiality or integrity effect. Whether a given deployment loses the process or only the connection depends on the consumer's goroutine layout, which is outside this repository. No Go toolchain is available on this host, so the panic was traced in code rather than reproduced.

findings.title: Cross-type $ref backtrack callback panics the loader on a crafted OpenAPI document
findings.impact: Any process that loads an OpenAPI document it did not author dies on a document of this shape: openapi3.Loader offers no recover, and grep confirms none exists anywhere in the module. That covers this repository's own cmd/validate, and any service, linter, gateway, diff tool or documentation portal that accepts a user-supplied specification. Where the load happens inside a net/http handler the panic is recovered per connection; where it happens at startup, in a worker, or in a CLI, the process terminates.
findings.preconditions: The attacker controls the bytes of the OpenAPI document that is loaded - the local-app.md §0 principal 'a file the tool is pointed at'. No external $refs are needed: the crafted document is entirely self-contained, so IsExternalRefsAllowed can stay false. No network access and no privileges are required.
findings.recommendation: Key the visited set and the backtrack map on the pair (ref string, component type) rather than on the ref string alone, so a Header reference and a Response reference to the same location never share a queue. As a defence in depth that is cheap and independent, convert all ten backtrack closures to the comma-ok form and have the mismatch return the existing errMUST* error for that component kind rather than panicking - a document that points two component types at one node is malformed, and rejecting it with an error is the intended outcome. Add a loader test with the document above and one with the ParameterRef/SchemaRef pairing.

triage.reason: The strict type gate at loader.go:540 is the control, and loader.go:546 is the documented path around it: the map[string]any branch JSON round-trips the node into whichever type the caller asked for, and shouldVisitRef returns before either branch runs. No recover() exists in the module.
The whole document is the input; cmd/validate/main.go:47 reads it from a path the invoker names, and Loader.LoadFromData/LoadFromIoReader accept arbitrary bytes.
A single-value type assertion panics on mismatch by Go's definition.
loader.go is a non-test file in the published module; ResolveRefsIn runs on every LoadFromData, LoadFromFile and LoadFromURI.

The boundary is document author to loading process (local-app.md §0: a file the tool is pointed at). cmd/validate is the in-repository proof that a document from outside the operator is a supported input.

The extension-node path is not an artefact of my reading: loader.go:462-468 documents the '$ref to a top-level key lands in T.Extensions' case as an intentional feature (issue856), and loader.go:562-565 documents the round-trip that follows it.

The attacker gains process termination in the CLI and worker cases, which is not marginal; severity stays at medium because the most common server deployment recovers per connection and because no confidentiality or integrity effect is claimed.

findings.limits: Establishes an unrecovered panic during document loading. It does not establish memory disclosure, code execution, or any effect on a document the operator authored. Traced in code, not reproduced: no Go toolchain is present on this host.

findings.title: SchemaError.Error() panics instead of degrading when the rejected value cannot be JSON-encoded

location.component: openapi3 schema error rendering, reached from every openapi3filter error path

findings.impact: An unauthenticated remote client turns a routine 400-class validation failure into a Go panic, deterministically and with a two-byte body - no map-ordering luck, unlike F-001. Because the panic fires while the consumer is logging or encoding the error, it can land outside whatever recover the request path has. Under net/http the request is aborted and the connection closed; off that path, the process terminates.
findings.preconditions: The operation declares a request body (or a response, symmetrically) with content type application/yaml or application/x-yaml and a non-empty schema; the served document is OpenAPI 3.0.x; and the caller renders the returned error - which both shipped entry points do by default. SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled must be left at its default false. For an OpenAPI 3.1+ document openapi3filter adds EnableJSONSchema2020 (validate_request.go:359-361), and VisitJSON then routes to the santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema validator (schema.go:1945-1947, schema_jsonschema_validator.go), which does not build the SchemaError at schema.go:2045 - so 3.1 documents reach this sink only when schema compilation fails and useJSONSchema2020 falls back to visitJSON.
findings.recommendation: Never panic while formatting an error. Replace both `panic(err)` calls with a fallback rendering, e.g. write `fmt.Sprintf("%#v", err.Value)` or a fixed `<unencodable value>` marker when Encode fails; an Error() method that can panic makes every error handler in every consumer a crash site. Separately, normalise at the boundary: have YamlBodyDecoder (req_resp_decoder.go:1439) convert map[any]any to map[string]any recursively and reject non-string keys with a ParseError, so no non-JSON value ever enters the schema layer - that also removes the need for the map[any]any branch at schema.go:2023.
findings.inference: That github.com/oasdiff/yaml3 decodes a mapping with a non-string key into map[any]any rather than erroring or coercing. I read that from this repository's own handling - the dedicated `case map[any]any` branch at schema.go:2023 with its issue-444 comment, which exists only because the decoder produces that type - and not by running the decoder, which this host cannot do.
findings.what_would_settle_it: A test in openapi3filter that calls YamlBodyDecoder with the body `1: a` and asserts the concrete type of the returned value, or the mapping-decode path of github.com/oasdiff/yaml3 (the isStringMap branch in its decoder), neither of which is present in the target tree.

triage.reason: No recover() exists in the module, and no caller can avoid the sink: rendering the error is the only way to use it, and both shipped entry points render it by default.
err.Value is the decoded request body, taken verbatim from the wire at openapi3filter/validate_request.go:329 and passed to VisitJSON at :364.

encoding/json's newMapEncoder returns an unsupportedTypeEncoder for a map whose key kind is Interface, so Encode returns an error rather than emitting anything; the following line converts that error into a panic unconditionally.
SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled is a package variable initialised to false at schema.go:34; the branch ships enabled and no build tag guards it.
Remote HTTP client to server process.

A deployment could set SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled = true at init, or terminate YAML at a gateway before it reaches the validator. No such control is in this repository and no exported artifact was supplied, so per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS - which is one of the two reasons this finding is probable rather than confirmed.
The attacker gains deterministic termination of request handling from an unauthenticated position; that is not a marginal capability.

findings.limits: Availability only. It does not establish that the panic escapes net/http's recover in a given deployment, nor any confidentiality or integrity effect. Scoped to OpenAPI 3.0.x documents: an adversarial re-reading of the assertion against the code narrowed it, because 3.1 documents take the JSON Schema 2020-12 path and only fall back to visitJSON when schema compilation fails. Both the decoder's output type and the effect of FP-08 remain open, and each is named above.

findings.title: The encoded-path-separator gate is enforced by ValidationHandler and not by the Validator middleware
findings.evidence:
Two shipped entry points reach the same effect - resolve a request to an operation, validate it including its security requirements, then pass it to the wrapped handler - and only one carries the gate.

ValidationHandler.validateRequest (validation_handler.go:89-116):
   91  route, pathParams, err := h.router.FindRoute(r)
   96  if err := h.checkEncodedPathSeparator(r, route); err != nil { return err }
  111  if err = ValidateRequest(r.Context(), requestValidationInput); err != nil { return err }

Validator.Middleware (middleware.go:120-147):
  122  route, pathParams, err := v.router.FindRoute(r)
  134  if err = ValidateRequest(ctx, requestValidationInput); err != nil { ... }
  147  h.ServeHTTP(wr, r)

The gate's own doc comment states the risk it exists to close (validation_handler.go:118-122): 'The router matches on the decoded path while routers such as gorilla/mux with UseEncodedPath match on the escaped one, so the operation validated here - its security requirements included - would not be the operation the wrapped handler serves.' `grep -rn 'checkEncodedPathSeparator|ErrEncodedPathSeparator' --include='*.go' .` returns hits only in validation_handler.go; nothing in middleware.go, in either router, or in ValidateRequest applies an equivalent check.
The asymmetry matters because the ungated sibling is the one the documentation teaches: README.md:109 and :134 both build routers/gorillamux, whose NewRouter calls `mux.NewRouter().UseEncodedPath()` (routers/gorillamux/router.go:57), i.e. it matches on r.URL.EscapedPath(). ValidationHandler, the gated sibling, hardcodes the legacy router instead (validation_handler.go:40), which matches on the decoded url.Path (routers/legacy/router.go:118-141). With `/public/{name}` unauthenticated and a second operation reachable only after decoding, a request for `/public/a%2Fb` is matched by gorillamux against the escaped path - `[^/]+` accepts `a%2Fb` - while a downstream handler reading r.URL.Path sees `/public/a/b`.
findings.impact: Where it lands, the security requirements and the parameter and body schema of one operation are enforced while a different operation is served: an operation whose spec declares no `security` can be validated in place of one that does, which is an authorization bypass rather than a validation gap. Where the two routers happen to agree, there is no effect.
findings.preconditions: A deployment uses Validator.Middleware (or bare ValidateRequest, as the README example does) with a router whose path matching differs from the wrapped handler's - the canonical case being gorillamux with UseEncodedPath in front of a handler that reads the decoded r.URL.Path - and the document contains at least two operations that the escaped and decoded forms of one request resolve to differently.
findings.recommendation: Move the check out of ValidationHandler and into the shared path so both entry points inherit it: either call it from Validator.Middleware immediately after FindRoute, or - better, since bare ValidateRequest is what the README teaches - fold it into ValidateRequest itself, gated on RequestValidationInput.Route being non-nil, and export the behaviour as an Option for consumers who intentionally allow encoded separators. Add the mirror of the existing ValidationHandler coverage against Validator.Middleware so the two cannot drift apart again.
findings.inference: That a real deployment pairs an escaped-path-matching router with a decoded-path-matching downstream handler. Every ingredient is in this repository - gorillamux uses UseEncodedPath, the legacy router uses the decoded path, the README teaches gorillamux, and the library itself documents the divergence - but no wired-up pair of the two is present here, so the last step from asymmetry to exploited bypass is argued rather than observed.
findings.what_would_settle_it: An integration test in openapi3filter that drives Validator.Middleware with a gorillamux router over a document with one unauthenticated and one authenticated operation, sends a path containing %2F, and asserts which operation was validated against which was served - the direct mirror of the ErrEncodedPathSeparator coverage that already exists for ValidationHandler.

triage.reason: No shared layer applies the gate: grep shows checkEncodedPathSeparator is referenced only from validation_handler.go:96, and neither router nor ValidateRequest performs an equivalent comparison.

A reverse proxy or ingress that rejects or normalises %2F before the application would close this. No such artifact exists in the repository and none was supplied, so per FP-08 the answer is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS. This is what caps the finding at probable.
The two are not different constructs that merely look alike: middleware.go:119 and validation_handler.go:65 both return an http.Handler that validates and then delegates, and both are exported API.

findings.limits: Establishes that a control present on one entry point is absent from its sibling, and that the library itself documents the class the control addresses. It does not demonstrate a concrete bypass against a running pair of routers, and it makes no claim about deployments whose downstream handler matches on the escaped path.

findings.title: External $ref resolution reads any URL or local path with no scheme or host policy and no client timeout
findings.impact: A crafted OpenAPI document makes the loading process issue GET requests from its own network position - cloud instance metadata, internal admin interfaces, anything reachable from the host - and read arbitrary local files into the parsed document, from where their contents can surface in validation errors, in a re-serialised document, or in a diff. Denial of service through a hanging fetch is available with no crafting at all.
findings.preconditions: The consumer sets IsExternalRefsAllowed (as the README quickstart does) or installs a permissive custom ReadFromURIFunc, and loads a document whose bytes an attacker influenced. The default IsExternalRefsAllowed=false blocks all of this, which is why the finding is bounded to medium.
findings.recommendation: Give the built-in reader a policy surface rather than a boolean: an optional allowlist of schemes and hosts and an optional base directory that ReadFromFile must contain after resolving symlinks, both enforced after each redirect rather than only on the first URL. Ship ReadFromHTTP with an http.Client that has a Timeout, and build the request with http.NewRequestWithContext(loader.Context, ...) so cancellation works. Change the README quickstart so IsExternalRefsAllowed is not the default posture shown to new users, and carry the SECURITY note already written on the ReadFromURIFunc field onto the IsExternalRefsAllowed field, where the reader of the quickstart will meet it.
findings.inference: That a consumer enables IsExternalRefsAllowed while loading a document it did not author. The README quickstart makes that combination the documented starting point, but no such consumer is present in this repository, so the step from 'the code will fetch anything' to 'a real deployment fetches attacker-chosen targets' is argued rather than observed.
findings.what_would_settle_it: Any consumer of openapi3.Loader that sets IsExternalRefsAllowed on a document path that is not fully operator-controlled - a gateway, a linting service, a CI job validating submitted specs. Inside this repository, a test that starts a local listener, loads a document whose $ref points at it, and asserts the connection arrives would settle the code half without any remote target.

triage.reason: IsExternalRefsAllowed is the only control and it is binary: loader.go:114-119 either refuses every external ref or permits every one. There is no layer between the permitted state and os.ReadFile / http.DefaultClient.Do, and loader.go:389-393 disables even that check whenever a custom ReadFromURIFunc is installed.
The URL is the $ref string taken from the document; resolvePathWithRef (loader.go:362-371) passes it to url.Parse and then straight to the reader with no constraint on scheme, host or path.

Reading other files is the declared purpose of the flag, so the exposure is intended - but per FP-05 the finding moves rather than disappears: what is not bounded is WHICH locations may be read. It moves to the absence of any scheme, host, redirect or base-directory constraint behind the intended exposure, and to the missing client timeout at loader_uri_reader.go:46, which no reading of the flag's intent covers. Severity is held at medium for this reason.

Network egress policy - an outbound proxy, a container network policy, a metadata-service hop limit - lives outside this repository and no artifact was supplied, so per FP-08 this cannot be answered HOLDS.

findings.limits: Establishes the absence of a read policy and of a timeout in code. It does not demonstrate a fetch against any real target: no remote testing was authorized and none was attempted. It says nothing about deployments that leave IsExternalRefsAllowed at its safe default.

findings.title: CI executes third-party tooling resolved at @latest in jobs that export GITHUB_TOKEN and declare no permissions block
findings.evidence:
The build-and-test job exports the token to every step in the job:

    8   env:
   10     GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

and `grep -rn permissions .github/workflows/` returns nothing, so both jobs inherit the repository default rather than declaring least privilege (INF-15).
In that same job, and in the second job, code fetched from a mutable @latest reference is downloaded and executed against the checked-out tree:

   59   - run: go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/modernize/cmd/modernize@latest -test -diff -fix -omitzero=false ./...
   99   - run: go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/nilness/cmd/nilness@latest ./...
  128   - run: go run -a github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/cmd/validate@latest -- openapi3/testdata/test.openapi.yml
  202   - run: go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest
  204   - run: find . -type f -iname '*.go' ! -iname '*.pb.go' -exec goimports-reviser {} \;

Line 59 runs an @latest tool with -fix, i.e. it is granted write access to the source tree, and line 202 installs a third-party binary outside the getkin and golang organisations and then runs it over every Go file.
Every action reference is a mutable tag, none is a 40-character SHA (INF-16, SUP-09): actions/setup-go@v6 (:28, :199), actions/cache@v3 (:33), actions/checkout@v6 (:43, :198), actions/checkout@v2 (shellcheck.yml:12), ludeeus/action-shellcheck@1.1.0 (shellcheck.yml:15). Pinned by SHA: 0 of 6.
findings.impact: A compromise of any of these upstreams - the x/tools module, the incu6us/goimports-reviser module, or any of the five tagged actions - executes attacker code inside a job that has the repository checked out, has GITHUB_TOKEN in its environment, and in one case is explicitly invoked with a flag that rewrites source files. The blast radius reaches from tampering with the tree that later releases are cut from, up to whatever the effective token permissions allow.
findings.preconditions: An upstream compromise, which is the threat model this class exists for rather than an attacker-controlled step. On the pull_request trigger from a fork GitHub restricts the token to read-only, so the meaningful exposure is on push events and same-repository pull requests, where the default token permissions apply.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit `permissions:` block - `contents: read` is sufficient for both jobs as written - so the job stops inheriting whatever the repository default is. Replace every @latest with a pinned module version, and prefer a `tools.go` plus go.mod entries so the versions are locked and dependabot-visible; go run's -fix step in particular should not be resolvable to code nobody has reviewed. Pin all five actions by 40-character commit SHA with the tag in a trailing comment, and bring shellcheck.yml's actions/checkout@v2 up to the same version as the other workflow.
findings.inference: The effective permissions of secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN in this repository. GitHub resolves them from the repository or organisation 'Default workflow permissions' setting, which is not an artifact in the tree, so whether a compromised step could write to the repository or only read it is inferred from the absence of a permissions block rather than observed.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The repository's Settings > Actions > General > Default workflow permissions value (read-only versus read-and-write), or simply an added top-level `permissions: contents: read` block, which makes the question moot by fixing the answer in the tree.

triage.reason: No control in the repository restricts what these steps may do: there is no permissions block, no environment with reviewers, and no step that verifies a hash or signature of anything it downloads.

The boundary is upstream maintainer to this project's CI. Only cmd/validate@latest at :128 points back inside the same owner (getkin) and is therefore hardening rather than third-party risk per SUP-09; x/tools, incu6us/goimports-reviser, ludeeus/action-shellcheck and the actions/* references all cross it.

The default GITHUB_TOKEN permission and any organisation ruleset that forbids unpinned actions live outside the repository. INF-15 states this explicitly: check it, because you cannot assume it in either direction. No exported artifact arrived, so UNKNOWN, which caps the finding at probable.

This is not defence in depth that happens to be absent: three separate steps execute unreviewed third-party code with the tree checked out, and one of them is given -fix. What is bounded is the token's reach, not the code execution, and that bound is exactly what FP-08 leaves UNKNOWN.

findings.limits: No upstream is asserted to be compromised, and no dependency advisory was consulted (the engagement forbids it). This is a statement about the pipeline's exposure, not about any incident. Self-hosted runners are not in use: every runs-on is a GitHub-hosted image (:17-20, :196, shellcheck.yml:9), so the INF-16 runner half does not apply.

findings.title: Request and response bodies are buffered whole with no size limit and no option to impose one
findings.evidence:
Every body path reads to EOF with no cap, and the public surface offers no way to set one:
  openapi3filter/validate_request.go:276  data, err = io.ReadAll(req.Body)
  openapi3filter/validate_request.go:453  data, err = io.ReadAll(input.Request.Body)   (a second full copy, for AuthenticationFunc)
  openapi3filter/validate_response.go:131 data, err := io.ReadAll(body)
  openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1420 PlainBodyDecoder
  openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1477 UrlencodedBodyDecoder
  openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1675 FileBodyDecoder
openapi3filter/options.go declares fifteen Options fields and none of them bounds a body. On the response side the middleware buffers the entire response in memory before validating it (middleware.go:195 io.MultiWriter into wr.body for the warn wrapper, :256 wr.body.Write for the strict wrapper), which also defeats streaming for any response the wrapped handler produces.
Security requirement validation reads the body a second time and keeps both copies live (validate_request.go:447-460), so a body of size N can be resident twice before any schema is consulted.
findings.impact: None demonstrated and none claimed: a Go HTTP handler that reads its own body has the same property, and bounding the body is conventionally the consumer's job through http.MaxBytesReader. The note is that this library takes over body handling from the consumer and then provides no place to express the bound, and its README never tells the consumer to add one - so the quickstart path buffers without limit by construction.
findings.preconditions: Not applicable: no exploit path is asserted.
findings.recommendation: Add a MaxBodyBytes field to openapi3filter.Options and wrap req.Body in io.LimitReader (or http.MaxBytesReader when the ResponseWriter is available) before every io.ReadAll, returning a RequestError that maps to 413. Give it a documented non-zero default so consumers who read only the quickstart inherit a bound rather than none. Avoid the second full copy in validateSecurityRequirement by reusing the buffer ValidateRequestBody already holds. At minimum, add one line to the README's validation example showing http.MaxBytesReader around r.Body.

triage.reason: The body is the request body, wholly attacker-supplied.
The boundary is library to consumer (local-app.md §0: the application that imports it inherits the default), and behind it remote client to server.

The impact does not reach the user because the control is the consumer's to add and is standard practice in every Go HTTP service: net/http imposes no body limit either. Per FP-10 the finding stays written down and is downgraded rather than deleted - it is recorded as hardening at low severity because the missing piece is the option, not the check.

findings.limits: Asserts no exploit path. It records an API-default gap and the absence of any knob, not a demonstrated denial of service.

findings.title: ZipFileBodyDecoder expands archive entries with no size or entry-count limit
findings.evidence:
The decoder buffers the compressed body, then appends every entry's decompressed bytes into one slice with no ceiling:

  1684 func ZipFileBodyDecoder(body io.Reader, ...) (any, error) {
  1686   size, err := io.Copy(buff, body)
  1691   zr, err := zip.NewReader(bytes.NewReader(buff.Bytes()), size)
  1697   content := make([]byte, 0, bufferSize*len(zr.File))
  1700   for _, f := range zr.File {
  1713       content = append(content, buffer[:n]...)

Neither the total decompressed size nor the number of entries is bounded, so the compression ratio of the input decides the allocation. The preallocation at :1697 is itself proportional to the attacker-chosen entry count. The hazard is stated in the function's own doc comment at :1683 ('Use with caution as this implementation may be susceptible to a zip bomb attack'), and the decoder is not registered by default - the init at :1402-1417 registers fourteen media types and this is not one of them, so a consumer must call RegisterBodyDecoder to reach it.
findings.impact: None demonstrated and none claimed here: the decoder is opt-in and its risk is documented at the point of use. Recorded because a consumer that registers it inherits a body-to-memory amplification with no ceiling, and because the accompanying warning offers no safe alternative.
findings.preconditions: Not applicable: no exploit path is asserted. A consumer must first call RegisterBodyDecoder for a zip media type.
findings.recommendation: Bound the expansion rather than only warning about it: cap len(zr.File), wrap each entry's reader in io.LimitReader with a per-entry ceiling, and abort once the running total of decompressed bytes exceeds a limit or the ratio to `size` exceeds a threshold. Make those limits parameters of a constructor - NewZipFileBodyDecoder(maxEntries, maxTotalBytes) - so the registered decoder carries a bound by construction, and keep the existing free function as a deprecated alias.

triage.reason: The archive is the request body.
It is exported, non-test code in the published module; it is simply not registered by default (req_resp_decoder.go:1402-1417).

The exposure is intended and declared: the doc comment at req_resp_decoder.go:1683 names the zip-bomb risk, and reaching the decoder requires an explicit RegisterBodyDecoder call by the consumer. Per FP-05 the finding moves rather than disappearing - it moves to the absence of any bounded variant behind the intended opt-in.
The impact does not reach the user without a deliberate consumer choice made against a written warning, so this is recorded as hardening at low severity rather than as a denial-of-service finding.

findings.limits: Asserts no exploit path against any default configuration. No zip bomb was constructed or run; the reading is from the source only.

findings.title: Compiled regular expressions are cached in a package-global map that is never evicted
findings.evidence:
Every distinct `pattern` string ever compiled is stored forever in a package-level sync.Map:

  openapi3/schema.go:46      compiledPatterns sync.Map
  openapi3/schema_pattern.go:36  compiledPatterns.Store(pattern, cp)

The key is the pattern text, the value is the compiled matcher, and no code path deletes from the map - `grep -n compiledPatterns openapi3/*.go` returns only the declaration, one Load at schema.go:2727 and this Store. The cache is global rather than per-document or per-loader, so it is shared across every document a process ever loads. schema_pattern.go:15 already records that the surrounding code is racy with respect to writes to schema.Pattern.
findings.impact: None demonstrated and none claimed. In the normal case - one process, a fixed set of documents - the map is bounded by the specifications the operator ships. In a process that loads many documents it did not author, memory grows monotonically with the number of distinct pattern strings those documents contain, and the growth is keyed on attacker-supplied text.
findings.preconditions: Not applicable: no exploit path is asserted. The growth only matters for a long-lived process that loads unbounded numbers of third-party documents.
findings.recommendation: Scope the cache to the document or the loader rather than the package, or give the global a bounded eviction policy. Either removes the cross-document sharing that makes the growth unbounded, and the per-document form also removes the race the file's own comment records.

triage.reason: The key is schema.Pattern, taken verbatim from the loaded document.
The boundary is document author to loading process, the same principal as F-002.

The impact does not reach the user in the ordinary single-tenant case, where the pattern set is fixed by the operator's own specifications. Downgraded to hardening at low severity rather than deleted, because the multi-document case is real and the fix is small.

findings.limits: Asserts no exploit path. No memory measurement was taken - there is no Go toolchain on this host - so the rate of growth is not quantified.

findings.title: An AWS access key identifier is tracked in a third-party test fixture
findings.evidence: A scan of the whole tree for high-precision secret formats (`ghp_`, `AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}`, `sk-ant-`, PEM private-key headers, `xox[baprs]-`) returned exactly one hit: a presigned S3 URL inside a third-party OpenAPI example document, carrying `X-Amz-Credential=[REDACTED:secret]/20170728/us-west-2/s3/aws4_request` together with `X-Amz-Date=20170728T...`, `X-Amz-Expires=3600` and an `X-Amz-Signature`. A second scan for `(password|secret|api[_-]?key|token)\s*[:=]\s*"..."` across non-test Go files returned nothing. The value is an AWS access key identifier, not a secret access key; the signature it accompanies expired one hour after 2017-07-28.
findings.impact: None: an access key identifier is not a credential on its own, the presigned signature it belongs to expired in 2017, and the document is a vendored example specification rather than this project's own configuration. Recorded because supply-chain-secrets-malware.md §8 applies to every repository and a credential-shaped string in the tree should be named rather than silently passed over, and because a scanner run by a downstream consumer will flag it again.
findings.preconditions: Not applicable: no exploit path is asserted.
findings.recommendation: Leave the fixture functionally as it is, but replace the identifier and signature with obvious placeholders so the file stops tripping secret scanners in this repository and in every consumer that vendors it. If it is kept verbatim to preserve fidelity with the upstream sample, add a scanner allowlist entry naming the file and the reason.

triage.reason: The path does not exist in what ships as code: openapi3/testdata/ is fixture data consumed only by _test.go files, and Go excludes testdata from the build of any importing module.

The data has no security value: an AWS access key ID is an identifier, not a secret, and the presigned URL carrying it declares X-Amz-Expires=3600 against an X-Amz-Date in 2017, so the signature it authenticates is long expired. The record belongs to a third-party sample specification, not to this project.

findings.limits: No attempt was made to use the identifier, and none should be: that would be an unauthorized test against a third party. Whether the key ID still exists in the issuing account is not knowable from this tree and was not investigated.

ruled_out.class: SQL, NoSQL and OS command injection (WEB-07, WEB-08)
ruled_out.where: Whole tree. No data-access layer, query builder or process execution exists: grep for os/exec, database/sql, exec.Command and Runtime across all 293 Go files returns no hit, and go.mod declares no database or shell driver. The library never reaches a query or a shell, so the class has no sink here.
Whole tree. No template engine is imported and no HTML is produced; the only rendering is error text through fmt and encoding/json.

openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1402-1417 and openapi3/loader.go. The registered decoders are encoding/json, oasdiff/yaml3, mime/multipart, net/url, encoding/csv and raw byte readers - pure data formats with no dynamic type resolution and no constructor invocation. The reflection in openapi3/loader.go:629-681 and openapi3/helpers.go:208-229 only reads struct fields and map keys; it instantiates nothing named by the document.

ruled_out.class: Prompt injection and agent-instruction files inside the target (AI-22)
ruled_out.where: Whole tree, three levels deep. No CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .mcp.json, .cursor/ or copilot-instructions file exists; .gitignore:24 lists .claude/ but no such directory is present. No file in the target addressed instructions to the reviewer, and none was acted on.

ruled_out.class: Route confusion from path-template collisions in the legacy router
ruled_out.where: routers/legacy/router.go:141-169 with openapi3/paths.go:64-75. Two templates differing only in variable name ('/a/{x}' and '/a/{y}') collapse to one trie node, because pathpattern.EqualSuffix compares Kind and Pattern and a variable suffix has an empty Pattern, so the terminal node's VariableNames is overwritten by whichever Add ran last over a randomly ordered map. Paths.Validate rejects that document first: normalizeTemplatedPath erases variable names and newConflictingPaths fires on the duplicate, and legacy.NewRouter calls doc.Validate before building the trie (routers/legacy/router.go:62). Bound: this covers the legacy router only. gorillamux.NewRouter does not validate the document - it says 'Assumes spec is .Validate()d' at routers/gorillamux/router.go:50 - so an unvalidated document there was not exercised.

ruled_out.class: Unbounded allocation from attacker-chosen array indexes in deepObject parameters
ruled_out.where: openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:975-1017. A query such as 'p[arr][2000000000]=x' would once have driven an allocation proportional to the index. maxSliceMapToSliceGap = 10000 is enforced at :1006 before the loop that builds the slice, and it bounds the gap between the largest index and the number of supplied items rather than the index alone, so the check cannot be walked past by supplying more items.

ruled_out.class: Recompilation of a regular expression per attacker-supplied query key
ruled_out.where: openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:697-707. The deepObject prefix matcher is compiled once outside the loop over url.Values, with the reason recorded in the comment at :698-701, so the number of query keys no longer multiplies regexp compilation.

ruled_out.class: Catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS) through schema pattern or format validation
ruled_out.where: openapi3/schema_pattern.go:21 and openapi3/schema_formats.go:111. Both compile with the standard library regexp package, whose RE2 engine runs in time linear in the input and has no backtracking. A consumer that installs a custom RegexCompilerFunc (openapi3/schema_validation_settings.go:10) owns that property instead; that configuration is not present in this repository. Bound: refutes the engine, not a pathological pattern under a substituted engine.

openapi3filter/validate_request.go:436-439. When Options.AuthenticationFunc is nil, validateSecurityRequirement returns ErrAuthenticationServiceMissing rather than allowing the request, so a consumer that forgets to wire authentication gets a failure, not a bypass. README.md:341 records that ValidationHandler.AuthenticationFunc was deliberately changed to stop defaulting to the noop implementation. Security requirements are also evaluated before parameters and body (validate_request.go:45-59), so an unauthenticated request cannot reach the decoders of an authenticated operation.

ruled_out.class: Dependency vulnerabilities in the declared module graph (SUP-13, SUP-14)
ruled_out.where: go.mod and go.sum were read; six direct and seven indirect dependencies are declared with pinned versions and go.sum hashes. No reachability or advisory analysis was performed: the engagement forbids consulting an advisory database, upstream repository or issue tracker, and no Go toolchain exists on this host, so govulncheck - the one tool SUP-13 names as having a real call graph - could not be run. Nothing is claimed about any dependency's vulnerability status in either direction.

ruled_out.class: Dynamic confirmation of the three panic findings
ruled_out.where: No Go toolchain is installed on this host ('go not found'), so F-001, F-002 and F-003 could not be reproduced by a test. Each was traced from attacker-controlled source to sink in code that is in the target tree, and F-003 additionally rests on the output type of a third-party decoder, which is named in its inference field. What would unblock: a Go 1.25 toolchain and 'go test ./openapi3filter/... ./openapi3/...' with the three cases added.
